name: Sarvāstivāda
alt_names: Shuo yiqie you bu 說一切有部 (Chinese)

tradition.text: Arose in the third century after the parinirvāṇa by division from the Sthaviras (Vasumitra); the Abhidharma was fixed at the council of King Kaniṣka in Kashmir (Xuanzang)

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE (as a named school) – c. 10th c. CE in India; attested by inscriptions from the 1st c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the sūtras (Āgamas), the Vinaya and the mātṛkā lists
transmissions_received.evidence: Madhyamāgama (T26) and Saṃyuktāgama (T99) in Chinese; Sanskrit Āgama fragments from Turfan and Gilgit

transmissions_received.what: the Sthavira identity; the split into Sarvāstivāda and Haimavata

transmissions_given.what: Abhidharma categories (dharma lists, the path of seeing and cultivation, the nirvedhabhāgīyas) reworked in the Yogācārabhūmi and Abhidharmasamuccaya
the Abhidharmakośa and Vaibhāṣika scholasticism in China and Japan
shared Abhidharma (the seven books, the Kośa)
the framework of the path later expanded into the five paths; the bodhisattva career of three incalculable aeons

distinctive_positions: Everything exists (sarvam asti): dharmas of the past, present and future all exist as real entities (dravya); only the activity (kāritra) of a dharma distinguishes the times (AK 5.25–26).
Seventy-five dharmas in five groups (in the later scholastic count): matter, mind, mental factors, conditioned factors dissociated from mind, and three unconditioned dharmas.
Real dissociated factors: possession (prāpti) and non-possession, the four characteristics of the conditioned (birth, duration, decay, impermanence), the life faculty, homogeneity (AK 2.35–48).
Unmanifest matter (avijñapti-rūpa) carries vows and non-vows through time (AK 1.11, 4.13).
Six causes, four conditions and five results (AK 2.49–64).
Realization of the truths is gradual: sixteen moments, fifteen of which make up the path of seeing (AK 6.25–28).
An arhat can fall back from arhatship (six kinds of arhat, AK 6.56–60); a stream-enterer cannot.
An intermediate existence (antarābhava) links death and rebirth (AK 3.10–14).
The Abhidharma is the word of the Buddha, arranged by his disciples (Vaibhāṣika view reported by Yaśomitra).
The Buddha's physical body is impure (sāsrava); his dharmakāya is the pure qualities of the aśaikṣa.
summary: The Sarvāstivāda ('those who say everything exists') was the most influential Abhidharma school of northern India, centred in Mathurā, Kashmir and Gandhāra. Its canonical Abhidharma of seven books (the Jñānaprasthāna and six 'feet') was systematized in the Mahāvibhāṣā and summarized — and partly criticized — in Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośa, defended by Saṅghabhadra. Its categories and path structure became the base of later Indian, Tibetan and East Asian scholasticism.
notes: Parent set to lin:early-buddhism (umbrella) so that the school counts as its own root in convergence; its Sthavira ancestry is recorded under lin:sthavira. Relationship to the Mūlasarvāstivāda is disputed (see lin:mulasarvastivada).

name: Sautrāntika
alt_names: Sautrāntika ('those who take the sūtras as the end/authority')

tradition.text: Split from the Sarvāstivāda in the fourth century after the parinirvāṇa, claiming Ānanda as its teacher (Vasumitra)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–5th c. CE as a recognisable current

transmissions_received.what: the Abhidharma categories it criticized; membership of the Sarvāstivāda ordination lineage
the Dārṣṭāntika positions (e.g. mental karma as volition itself, rejection of avijñapti)

transmissions_given.what: the theory of seeds (bīja) and the specific transformation of the series, reworked as the storehouse consciousness
momentariness, the causeless destruction argument and the representationalist theory of perception used by Dignāga and Dharmakīrti (Sautrāntika tenets in Tibetan doxography)

distinctive_positions: Only the sūtras are authoritative; the Abhidharma treatises are works of disciples, not the word of the Buddha (Yaśomitra: 'ye sūtraprāmāṇikā na śāstraprāmāṇikāḥ te sautrāntikāḥ').
Only the present exists; past and future dharmas do not exist as entities: a conditioned thing 'arises having not been, and having been, ceases' (AKBh 5.27).
Everything conditioned is momentary; destruction has no cause (AKBh 4.2–3).

Karmic efficacy and latent defilements are carried as seeds (bīja) — capacities in the psycho-physical series that ripen through its specific transformation (santati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa) (AKBh 2.36, 5.2, ch. 9).
Possession (prāpti), the characteristics of the conditioned, avijñapti-rūpa and the unconditioned dharmas are designations, not real entities (AKBh 2.36, 2.46, 2.55, 4.3).
Cognition bears the form (ākāra) of its object; external objects are inferred, not directly grasped (later doxographic summary).
An arhat does not fall back from arhatship (AKBh 6.58).
summary: The Sautrāntikas were a critical current within the northern Sarvāstivāda ordination tradition that accepted only the sūtras as authoritative and reduced many of the Vaibhāṣika's real entities to designations. Their positions are known mainly through Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Yaśomitra's commentary and Saṅghabhadra's refutations; they shaped Yogācāra (seeds) and the Buddhist logicians (momentariness, representationalism).
notes: The relation between the earlier 'Dārṣṭāntikas' of the Mahāvibhāṣā and the later 'Sautrāntikas' is not settled; Tibetan doxography (grub mtha') systematizes Sautrāntika tenets differently from the Indian sources. Parent set to Sarvāstivāda (tradition: split from it).

name: Mahāsāṃghika

tradition.text: Formed at the first schism, a century or more after the parinirvāṇa — according to the Sthavira accounts over the ten points of Vaiśālī or the five points of Mahādeva; according to its own account over the Sthaviras' enlargement of the Vinaya

scholarly.text: c. 4th–3rd c. BCE (first schism) – c. 7th c. CE and later

transmissions_given.what: the supramundane buddhology, the original purity of mind and the ten-stage bodhisattva career (much discussed as a source of Mahāyāna ideas; scholarly hypothesis)
the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya translated by Buddhabhadra and Faxian (used in early Chinese monasteries alongside other Vinayas)

distinctive_positions: The Buddhas are supramundane (lokottara); their bodies, powers and lifespans are without limit; the Buddha is always in concentration, never sleeps, and teaches all dharmas with a single sound (Vasumitra).
The mind is by nature luminous; it is defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Past and future do not exist as entities (Vasumitra).
There is no intermediate existence between death and rebirth (Vasumitra; Kathāvatthu 8.2 attributes the contrary view to others).
Stream-enterers can fall back; arhats cannot (Vasumitra).
Nine unconditioned dharmas (Vasumitra: the two cessations, space, the four formless spheres, the nature of dependent origination and of the noble path) — per Vasumitra, low confidence on the list.
The five points of Mahādeva on the imperfections of the arhat were accepted by the Mahāsāṃghika side according to the Sarvāstivāda accounts.
summary: The Mahāsāṃghika ('those of the great community') formed one side of the first schism of the Buddhist order, the other being the Sthaviras. It divided into several branches (Ekavyavahārika, Lokottaravāda, Kaukkuṭika/Gokulika, Bahuśrutīya, Prajñaptivāda, Caitika and the Andhra Śaila schools). Its Vinaya survives in Chinese and its Lokottaravāda branch's Mahāvastu in Sanskrit; its doctrines are known largely through Vasumitra's doxography.

name: Lokottaravāda
alt_names: Shuo chushi bu 說出世部 (Chinese)
regions: Middle Country (madhyadeśa, per the Mahāvastu colophon)

tradition.text: Branched from the Mahāsāṃghika in the second century after the parinirvāṇa (Vasumitra)

transmissions_received.evidence: Mahāvastu colophon: 'according to the recitation of the Lokottaravādin Mahāsāṃghikas of the Middle Country, the beginning of the Mahāvastu of the Vinaya Piṭaka' (Mvu i.2)

distinctive_positions: The Buddha's conduct, roots of merit, walking, standing, sitting and lying, his body, robes and food are all supramundane (Mvu i.167–168).
The Buddhas conform to the world (lokānuvartanā): they wash, eat, drink, take medicine and show old age though they have no dirt, hunger, thirst, illness or ageing (Mvu i.168–169).
The bodhisattva career runs through four conducts (caryā) and ten grounds (bhūmi) named durārohā … abhiṣeka (Mvu i.1, i.76).
The Mahāvastu belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka (its colophon), framing the Buddha's biography as the introduction to the monastic code.
summary: The Lokottaravāda, a branch of the Mahāsāṃghika, is named for its teaching that the Buddhas are 'beyond the world' (lokottara) and only appear to conform to worldly life. Its Sanskrit Vinaya texts survive: the Mahāvastu (a vast biography of the Buddha with jātakas and the ten bodhisattva grounds), the Prātimokṣa, the Bhikṣuṇī-Vinaya and the Abhisamācārikā.

name: Pudgalavāda
regions: Bengal and eastern India (Saṃmitīya per Xuanzang and Yijing)

tradition.text: The Vātsīputrīya split from the Sarvāstivāda (Vasumitra) or from the Theravāda's Vajjiputtakas (Dīpavaṃsa) in the third century after the parinirvāṇa

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE – c. 12th c. CE; the Saṃmitīya was one of the largest orders in 7th-c. India (Xuanzang)

distinctive_positions: There is a person (pudgala) that is neither the same as nor different from the aggregates; it is designated in dependence on the present, appropriated aggregates, as fire is designated in dependence on fuel (AKBh 9, Pradhan p. 461; Vasumitra).
The person is 'inexpressible' (avaktavya) — a fifth kind of knowable besides the past, the future, the present and the unconditioned (AKBh 9, p. 462–463).
Dharmas do not pass from one life to the next apart from the person; the person is the bearer of the burden of the aggregates (Bhārahāra-sūtra, as they read it).
Three designations of the person — by support, by transmigration and by cessation (Saṃmitīyanikāya-śāstra; low confidence on the terms).
Some conditioned things are momentary, others (e.g. the body) endure for a time (Vasumitra; low confidence).
An arhat can fall back (Kathāvatthu 1.2, per the commentary); an intermediate existence exists (Kathāvatthu 8.2, per the commentary: Sammitiyas).
summary: The Pudgalavāda ('those who affirm the person') comprised the Vātsīputrīya and its offshoots, above all the Saṃmitīya, which Xuanzang and Yijing describe as one of the four great orders of 7th-century India. They taught an inexpressible person, neither identical with nor different from the aggregates, and were refuted by the Theravāda (Kathāvatthu 1.1), the Sarvāstivāda (Vijñānakāya, Mahāvibhāṣā) and Vasubandhu (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya ch. 9). Few of their own texts survive, in Chinese.

name: Dharmaguptaka
regions: China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan (through its Vinaya)

tradition.text: Split from the Mahīśāsaka, claiming Maudgalyāyana as its teacher (Vasumitra); from the Mahiṃsāsaka (Dīpavaṃsa)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE – ; living through its Vinaya

transmissions_received.what: descent in Vasumitra's and the Pali lists

transmissions_given.what: the Four-Part Vinaya (Sifen lü) as the standard monastic code of East Asian Buddhism; the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī ordination lineages of China, Korea, Vietnam and Taiwan
the Four-Part Vinaya ordination brought to Japan by Jianzhen (Ganjin)

distinctive_positions: Though the Buddha is included in the Saṅgha, a gift to the Buddha yields greater fruit than a gift to the Saṅgha; offerings to stūpas bring great fruit (Vasumitra).
The liberation of the Buddha and of the disciples is one, though their paths differ (Vasumitra).
Outsiders (non-Buddhists) cannot obtain the five superknowledges (Vasumitra; low confidence).
The Four-Part Vinaya: 250 rules for bhikṣus and 348 for bhikṣuṇīs.
A canon in which the Dīrghāgama (T1) is affiliated with this school; a Bodhisattva Piṭaka and a Dhāraṇī Piṭaka are reported in its canon (low confidence).
summary: The Dharmaguptaka, a Sthavira-derived school of the north-west, is known above all for its Four-Part Vinaya (Sifen lü), translated into Chinese in 410–412, which became the monastic code of East Asian Buddhism and carries the only continuous bhikṣuṇī ordination lineage. The Chinese Dīrghāgama and the earliest Gāndhārī manuscripts (British Library) are associated with it.

name: Mūlasarvāstivāda
alt_names: Genben shuo yiqie you bu 根本說一切有部 (Chinese)
gzhi thams cad yod par smra ba (Tibetan)
regions: Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan, the Himalaya (through its Vinaya)

tradition.text: The 'root' (mūla) Sarvāstivāda, whose Vinaya was recited in the Buddha's time (Tibetan tradition)

scholarly.text: Vinaya compiled c. 1st–4th c. CE; named as a school from the 7th c. (Yijing); living through its Vinaya

transmissions_received.what: the Abhidharma of the seven books and the Kośa
transmissions_received.evidence: shared Abhidharma; Yijing reports the Mūlasarvāstivāda as one of four nikāyas

transmissions_given.what: the monastic ordination lineage brought by Śāntarakṣita (the 'lower Vinaya' line)
the Vinaya lines of the later spread
Vinaya study through Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra, one of the five great texts of the monastic curriculum

distinctive_positions: A very large Vinaya in seventeen sections (vastu) with a Vibhaṅga, Kṣudrakavastu and Uttaragrantha, rich in narratives (avadāna).
The only Indian Vinaya transmitted in Tibetan; the basis of all Tibetan monastic ordination.
Doctrinally at one with the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma (the Kośa is the Abhidharma of the Tibetan curriculum).
The bhikṣuṇī ordination of this Vinaya was never established in Tibet; whether it can be supplied from another Vinaya lineage is debated (recent).
Prātimokṣa: 258 rules in the Sanskrit text (the Tibetan tradition speaks of 253 vows of a gelong) — low confidence on both counts.
summary: The Mūlasarvāstivāda is known chiefly through its enormous Vinaya, preserved in Tibetan, partly in Chinese (Yijing) and in Sanskrit from the Gilgit manuscripts. Its relation to the Sarvāstivāda (identical, a later reorganisation, or a separate Mathurā-based group) is disputed. Its Vinaya is the living monastic code of Tibetan Buddhism.
notes: Parent set to Sarvāstivāda for convergence purposes; the tradition regards it as the root of which the others are branches. Scholarly views differ (identity, a later compilation, or a separate group).

name: Mahīśāsaka
regions: Sri Lanka (Faxian obtained its Vinaya there)

tradition.text: Split from the Sarvāstivāda (Vasumitra) or from the Theravāda (Dīpavaṃsa)

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE – c. 5th c. CE

distinctive_positions: Past and future do not exist; the present and the unconditioned exist (Vasumitra).
There is no intermediate existence (Vasumitra).
Since the Buddha is included in the Saṅgha, a gift to the Saṅgha yields great fruit, not a separate gift to the Buddha (Vasumitra).
Stream-enterers can fall back; arhats cannot (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Nine unconditioned dharmas including the 'suchness' of good, bad and neutral dharmas, of the path and of dependent origination (Vasumitra; low confidence on the list).
The Five-Part Vinaya (Wufen lü) with 251 rules for bhikṣus (low confidence on the count).
summary: The Mahīśāsaka was a Sthavira-derived school whose Five-Part Vinaya was brought from Sri Lanka by Faxian and translated into Chinese in 423–424. Vasumitra records a first group holding that only the present exists and a later group closer to Sarvāstivāda.

name: Sthavira (the Elders' group of the first schism)
alt_names: Theravāda in the wide sense of the Pali chronicles

tradition.text: The side of the elders at the first schism, a century or more after the parinirvāṇa

distinctive_positions: At the first schism the elders rejected the relaxations of Vinaya (Pali account) or the five points on the arhat (Vasumitra); the Mahāsāṃghika account says the elders enlarged the Vinaya.
All later Sthavira branches (Sarvāstivāda, Vibhajyavāda/Theravāda, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, Vātsīputrīya) trace themselves to this side of the split.
summary: A classificatory grouping: the 'Elders' who formed one side of the first schism of the Saṅgha against the Mahāsāṃghikas, and from whom the Sarvāstivāda, the Vibhajyavāda and Theravāda, the Mahīśāsaka, the Dharmaguptaka, the Kāśyapīya and the Pudgalavāda derived.
notes: A classificatory group: the member schools keep lin:early-buddhism as parent so that each counts as its own root in convergence. Recommend adding lin:sthavira to the merge's UMBRELLAS set.

name: Vaibhāṣika
distinctive_positions: The Abhidharma, arranged by Kātyāyanīputra and others from the Buddha's scattered teaching, is the word of the Buddha (Yaśomitra's report).
The orthodoxy of the Mahāvibhāṣā: real existence of dharmas in three times, prāpti, avijñapti, the four characteristics as real forces.
Vasubandhu presented the Kośa as 'mostly the Abhidharma as established by the Kashmiri Vaibhāṣikas' (AK 8.40).
summary: The Vaibhāṣikas ('followers of the Vibhāṣā') were the Kashmiri orthodoxy of the Sarvāstivāda, taking the Mahāvibhāṣā as authoritative. Saṅghabhadra's Nyāyānusāra defended their positions against the Sautrāntika criticisms of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

name: Dārṣṭāntika

scholarly.text: c. 1st c. BCE – 3rd c. CE (named in the Mahāvibhāṣā)

distinctive_positions: Mental karma is volition together with covetousness, malice and wrong view themselves (AKBh 4, Pradhan p. 237: 'abhidhyādaya eva manaskarmeti dārṣṭāntikāḥ').
Rejection of several Vaibhāṣika real entities (reported in the Mahāvibhāṣā).
Teaching by illustrative stories and examples (dṛṣṭānta), as in Kumāralāta's Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā.
summary: The Dārṣṭāntikas are a dissenting current within the Sarvāstivāda named and refuted in the Mahāvibhāṣā; they are generally regarded as forerunners of (or identical with) the later Sautrāntikas.

name: Haimavata
distinctive_positions: Vasumitra identifies the Haimavatas with the original Sthaviras, who withdrew to the Himalaya when the Sarvāstivāda became dominant.
The bodhisattva is an ordinary being (pṛthagjana) (Vasumitra; low confidence).
summary: A Sthavira branch that Vasumitra identifies with the original Elders displaced to the Himalaya by the Sarvāstivāda; listed among the later schools in the Pali chronicles.

name: Kāśyapīya
distinctive_positions: Past karma whose fruit has not yet ripened exists; past karma that has given its fruit, and the rest of the past, do not (Vasumitra; the Vibhajyavādin position of AKBh 5.25; Kathāvatthu 1.8 'some exist').
A Prātimokṣa survives in Chinese (T1460).
summary: A Sthavira branch (from the Sarvāstivāda in Vasumitra's list, from the Sabbatthivāda in the Pali list) holding that only unripened past karma exists; the Chinese Bieyi Saṃyuktāgama (T100) has been attributed to it.

name: Vibhajyavāda
distinctive_positions: Some of the past and future exist and some do not — distinguishing rather than affirming that everything exists (AKBh 5.25).
The mind is by nature luminous (reported and refuted in the Mahāvibhāṣā; low confidence on the attribution).
The Theravāda calls itself Vibhajjavāda (the Buddha is a 'vibhajjavādī', Mahāvaṃsa; Kathāvatthu commentary).
summary: A designation used in two ways: by the Sarvāstivāda for opponents who 'distinguish' which past and future things exist; by the Theravāda for itself. Modern accounts group the Theravāda, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka and Kāśyapīya as Vibhajyavādins (scholarly hypothesis).
notes: Classificatory label rather than a single ordination lineage.

name: Vātsīputrīya
distinctive_positions: The person is neither the aggregates nor other than them; it is designated in dependence on the aggregates (Vasumitra; AKBh 9).
Named in AKBh 9 as the holders of the pudgala doctrine ('vātsīputrīyāḥ pudgalaṃ santam icchanti', Pradhan p. 461).
summary: The root Pudgalavāda school, named after Vātsīputra; in Vasumitra's list it splits from the Sarvāstivāda and gives rise to the Dharmottarīya, Bhadrayānīya, Saṃmitīya and Ṣaṇṇagarika.

name: Saṃmitīya
distinctive_positions: The person is real, designated on the basis of the aggregates, neither the same as nor different from them (Saṃmitīyanikāya-śāstra).
Counted by Yijing among the four great nikāyas of India; by Xuanzang as present in very many monasteries (low confidence on figures).
Kathāvatthu commentary ascribes to the Sammitiyas the person (Kv 1.1) and the intermediate existence (Kv 8.2).
summary: The largest Pudgalavāda school, prominent in western and eastern India in the 7th century; one of the four nikāyas of Yijing and of the Tibetan four-group classification.

name: Dharmottarīya
distinctive_positions: Listed as a branch of the Vātsīputrīya (Vasumitra; Dīpavaṃsa); its own doctrines are not separately recorded.
summary: A Pudgalavāda branch named in all the major lists; no separate texts survive.

name: Bhadrayānīya
distinctive_positions: Listed as a branch of the Vātsīputrīya; no separate doctrines recorded beyond the school's list membership.
summary: A Pudgalavāda branch named in the lists of the eighteen schools.

name: Ṣaṇṇagarika
distinctive_positions: Listed as a branch of the Vātsīputrīya; no separate doctrines recorded.
summary: A Pudgalavāda branch named in the lists of the eighteen schools.

name: Ekavyavahārika
distinctive_positions: All dharmas are mere names (reported etymology: 'one utterance'); in Vasumitra its doctrines are said to agree with the Mahāsāṃghika (low confidence).
summary: An early branch of the Mahāsāṃghika in all lists.

name: Kaukkuṭika
distinctive_positions: Only the Abhidharma teaching is essential; the sūtra and vinaya are expedient (Vasumitra, per Xuanzang's version; low confidence).
summary: An early branch of the Mahāsāṃghika (Gokulika in the Pali lists).

name: Bahuśrutīya
distinctive_positions: The Buddha's teachings on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self and nirvāṇa are supramundane, the rest mundane (Vasumitra; low confidence).
Harivarman's Satyasiddhiśāstra is associated with this school in some Chinese accounts (disputed).
summary: A Mahāsāṃghika branch distinguishing the Buddha's supramundane from his mundane teachings.

name: Prajñaptivāda
distinctive_positions: Suffering is not an aggregate; the twelve sense-bases are not real (designations); conditioned things are designated in mutual dependence (Vasumitra; low confidence).
summary: A Mahāsāṃghika branch distinguishing what is real from what is designation (prajñapti).

name: Caitika
alt_names: Zhiduo shan bu 制多山部
distinctive_positions: Founded by a (second) Mahādeva who revived the five points at the end of the second century (Vasumitra); associated with caitya worship.
summary: A Mahāsāṃghika branch in all lists; in Vasumitra's account founded by a Mahādeva at a caitya hill; connected with the Andhra Śaila schools.

name: Pūrvaśaila
alt_names: Dongshan zhu bu 東山住部
distinctive_positions: Kathāvatthu commentary ascribes to the Pubbaseliyas (with the Aparaseliyas) that others can impute impurity to an arhat, that an arhat has ignorance and doubt, and is instructed by others (Kv 2.1–2.4) — the five points.
The Lokānuvartana-sūtra on the Buddha's conformity to the world is attributed to the Pūrvaśailas (low confidence).
summary: An Andhra branch of the Mahāsāṃghika (Amarāvatī, Nāgārjunakoṇḍa inscriptions), one of the Andhakas of the Pali commentary.

name: Aparaśaila
alt_names: Xishan zhu bu 西山住部
distinctive_positions: Shares the Pubbaseliya positions in the Kathāvatthu commentary (Kv 2.1–2.4).
summary: An Andhra branch of the Mahāsāṃghika, named with the Pūrvaśailas.

name: Andhaka
alt_names: the Andhra schools: Pubbaseliya, Aparaseliya, Rājagiriya, Siddhatthika (Pali commentary)
distinctive_positions: The Kathāvatthu commentary ascribes many of the refuted views to the Andhakas (low confidence on specific attributions).
summary: The Pali commentarial name for the Mahāsāṃghika-derived schools of Andhra.

name: Lü school (Vinaya school, Nanshan lineage)
alt_names: Nanshan lü zong 南山律宗

transmissions_given.what: the Nanshan Vinaya lineage taken to Japan by Jianzhen

distinctive_positions: The Four-Part (Dharmaguptaka) Vinaya is the standard code for all Chinese monastics.
Daoxuan interpreted the Vinaya in Mahāyāna terms (precepts grounded in the 'seed' of the mind; low confidence on details).
summary: The Chinese Vinaya school founded by Daoxuan on Zhongnan mountain, which made the Dharmaguptaka Four-Part Vinaya the monastic code of East Asia.

name: Ritsu-shū (Japanese Vinaya school)
distinctive_positions: Formal ordination on an ordination platform (kaidan) by the Four-Part Vinaya, introduced by Jianzhen; one of the six Nara schools.
summary: The Japanese Vinaya school established by Jianzhen (Ganjin), with its head temple Tōshōdaiji.

name: Jushe school (Abhidharmakośa school)
regions: Japan (one of the six Nara schools)
distinctive_positions: Study of the Abhidharmakośa in Paramārtha's (563–567) and Xuanzang's (651–654) translations as a preparatory discipline, later absorbed into Faxiang/Hossō study.
summary: The East Asian scholastic tradition of the Abhidharmakośa; in Japan the Kusha-shū, attached to the Hossō school.

name: Chengshi school (Satyasiddhi school)
regions: Japan (one of the six Nara schools, attached to Sanron)

transmissions_received.what: Harivarman's Satyasiddhiśāstra (affiliation with the Sautrāntika or the Bahuśrutīya is debated)

distinctive_positions: The Satyasiddhiśāstra teaches the emptiness of persons and of dharmas and was studied in China as a bridge to Mahāyāna until Jizang classed it as 'Hīnayāna'.
summary: The Chinese exegetical tradition centred on Harivarman's Satyasiddhiśāstra (translated by Kumārajīva, 411–412).
